Python through making

From a first line to a moving snake.

Sixteen hands-on mini-projects for Alex, designed for short lessons, pencil-first predictions, visible results, and one small win at a time.

8 weeks2 sessions / week30–45 minutesAges 9+
Jump to W1W2W3W4W5W6W7W8Finish

How to use this guide

Teach the next useful idea—not the whole chapter.

Each session ends with something Alex can run, change, and explain. The code is a starting point, not a script to memorize. If curiosity takes the project sideways, follow it.

Materials: a computer with Python and the built-in turtle module, paper, pencil, and a “bug log” notebook.

The 35-minute rhythm

  1. 5 min — Draw or predict on paper.
  2. 15 min — Build one working feature.
  3. 8 min — Change one thing and test it.
  4. 5 min — Read one bug out loud.
  5. 2 min — Demo and answer one question.
WEEK 01

Make the turtle move

Core ideas: commands, order, distance, angle, and reading the screen as feedback.

forward()right()done()
Session 1 · Project 01

The Mystery Path

30–35 minutes
1

Predict on paper

Draw where the turtle will end after each command. Mark its direction with an arrow.

2

Build

Type one command at a time. Run after every new line and compare the screen with the paper.

3

Change

Replace 90 with 60 or 120. Ask: “Does distance change direction?”

✓

Done when

Alex can point to the line that makes the turtle turn and predict its final direction.

Starter code
from turtle import *

forward(100)
right(90)
forward(60)
right(90)
forward(40)

done()
Session 2 · Project 02

Shape Detective

35–40 minutes
1

Plan

Draw a square. Label every side 100 and every turn 90°.

2

Build

Make the square using repeated commands. Leave repetition visible for now.

3

Investigate

Try a triangle with three 120° turns. Notice the total turn is always 360°.

?

Show & tell

“How did you know which angle would close the shape?”

Square and triangle clues
from turtle import *

# Square
forward(100); right(90)
forward(100); right(90)
forward(100); right(90)
forward(100); right(90)

# Move aside
penup(); forward(150); pendown()

# Triangle
forward(100); right(120)
forward(100); right(120)
forward(100); right(120)

done()
Parent cue:Do not correct the angle before running it. A shape that does not close is useful evidence, not failure.
WEEK 02

Give values a name

Core ideas: variables, input, text, numbers, and converting input with int().

variablesinput()int()
Session 1 · Project 03

Personal Shape Maker

35 minutes
1

Predict

Write: side = 80. Circle every place that should use the same value.

2

Build

Use one variable for all four sides and another for pen color.

3

Change

Edit the value once. Observe how four lines change together.

✓

Done when

Alex can explain that a variable is a named place holding a value.

Starter code
from turtle import *

side = 80
pen_color = "teal"
color(pen_color)

for step in range(4):
    forward(side)
    right(90)

done()
Session 2 · Project 04

Ask the Artist

35–45 minutes
1

Trace the data

Draw boxes for “answer as text” and “number after int().”

2

Build

Ask the player for a side length and use the answer to draw.

3

Test edges

Try 20, 100, and 200. What still fits on screen?

?

Show & tell

“Why did Python need int() before moving?”

Interactive version
from turtle import *

answer = input("How long should each side be? ")
side = int(answer)

for step in range(4):
    forward(side)
    right(90)

done()
Parent cue:If a letter causes an error in int(), read the last line of the error together. Save the fix for later; noticing the cause is enough.

Core ideas: arithmetic, comparison operators, Boolean answers, and using math to control a drawing.

Session 1 · Project 05

Number Lab

30–35 minutes
1

Predict

Solve five expressions on paper, including one with parentheses.

2

Check

Use print() as a lab instrument. Compare Python’s results with the predictions.

3

Compare

Ask Python questions that can only be True or False.

✓

Done when

Alex uses == to ask “is equal?” and = to store a value.

Experiment sheet
score = 7
bonus = 3

print(score + bonus)
print(score * 2)
print((score + bonus) * 2)
print(score > 5)
print(score == 10)
Session 2 · Project 06

Distance Challenge

35–40 minutes
1

Plan

Pick a target distance. Predict whether each test distance is “long enough.”

2

Build

Calculate a side length from two numbers, draw it, then print the comparison.

3

Stretch

Add a second question with and: long enough and short enough.

?

Show & tell

“What kind of answer does a comparison produce?”

Starter code
from turtle import *

base = 30
bonus = 25
distance = base + bonus

forward(distance)
print("Long enough?", distance >= 50)
print("Fits?", distance >= 40 and distance <= 100)

done()
Parent cue:Ask for a prediction before each run. A wrong prediction creates a better conversation than a correct guess made afterward.
WEEK 04

Let the program decide

Core ideas: if, elif, else, indentation, and mutually exclusive paths.

ifelifelse
Session 1 · Project 07

Color Gate

35–40 minutes
1

Act it out

Make three paper doors: red, blue, and “anything else.” Walk through exactly one.

2

Build

Ask for a color and let the answer choose the turtle’s pen.

3

Test

Run red, blue, and green. Record which branch runs each time.

✓

Done when

Only one branch runs, and Alex can show why indentation matters.

Decision code
from turtle import *

choice = input("Red, blue, or another color? ").lower()

if choice == "red":
    color("red")
elif choice == "blue":
    color("blue")
else:
    color("green")

circle(70)
done()
Session 2 · Project 08

Mini Quiz Show

35–45 minutes
1

Design

Write one fair question, one correct answer, and two response messages.

2

Build

Compare the answer after using lower(). Add or withhold a point.

3

Stretch

Add a second question and keep a running score.

?

Show & tell

“Which lines run when the answer is wrong?”

Quiz core
score = 0
answer = input("Which animal uses Python's turtle module? ")

if answer.lower() == "turtle":
    print("Correct!")
    score = score + 1
else:
    print("Good try. The answer is turtle.")

print("Score:", score)
Parent cue:Avoid nested conditions this week. One clean choice is more important than covering every possible kind of choice.
WEEK 05

Turn repetition into patterns

Core ideas: for loops, range(), a changing loop variable, and repeated visual rules.

forrange()repeat & change
Session 1 · Project 09

Loop Repair Shop

30–40 minutes
1

Spot the repeat

Underline the two lines repeated four times in Week 2’s square.

2

Refactor

Replace eight drawing lines with a two-line loop.

3

Generalize

Choose a number of sides and calculate the turn with 360 / sides.

✓

Done when

Changing one number makes a triangle, square, pentagon, or hexagon.

Any regular polygon
from turtle import *

sides = 6
turn = 360 / sides

for step in range(sides):
    forward(70)
    right(turn)

done()
Session 2 · Project 10

Spiral Studio

35–45 minutes
1

Predict

Sketch five lines where each new line is longer than the last.

2

Build

Use the loop variable as the distance so the pattern grows.

3

Art experiment

Try turns of 89, 91, 92, and 121 degrees. Save the most surprising.

?

Show & tell

“What repeats, and what changes each time?”

Growing spiral
from turtle import *

speed(0)
colors = ["navy", "tomato", "gold", "seagreen"]

for step in range(120):
    color(colors[step % 4])
    forward(step * 2)
    right(91)

done()
Parent cue:step % 4 can remain a “useful trick” for now. Explain only that it cycles through 0, 1, 2, 3.
WEEK 06

Package an idea as a function

Core ideas: defining, calling, and customizing functions with parameters.

defparametersreuse
Session 1 · Project 11

Shape Toolbox

35–40 minutes
1

Name the job

Circle the lines that belong to one job. Give that job a verb-first name.

2

Build

Create draw_square(size) and call it with three sizes.

3

Extend

Add a color parameter. Notice that the recipe stays the same while inputs change.

✓

Done when

The same function draws at least three different squares.

Reusable square
from turtle import *

def draw_square(size, pen_color):
    color(pen_color)
    for side in range(4):
        forward(size)
        right(90)

draw_square(40, "tomato")
draw_square(70, "seagreen")
draw_square(100, "navy")

done()
Session 2 · Project 12

Turtle Town

40–45 minutes
1

Storyboard

Draw a scene with a house, sun, and tree. Break it into named pieces.

2

Build

Create one function per object. Use goto(x, y) to place each piece.

3

Compose

Call the functions in a clear “scene setup” section at the bottom.

?

Show & tell

“How does your program show the plan for the whole scene?”

Scene-building pattern
from turtle import *

def move_to(x, y):
    penup(); goto(x, y); pendown()

def draw_house(size):
    for side in range(4):
        forward(size); right(90)
    left(45)
    for side in range(2):
        forward(size / 1.4); right(90)
    right(45)

def draw_sun(size):
    color("gold")
    circle(size)

move_to(-120, -40); draw_house(100)
move_to(120, 90); draw_sun(35)
done()
Parent cue:Let function names carry the meaning. Precise words such as draw_house and move_to make code easier to think about.
WEEK 07

Make code respond to a player

Core ideas: keyboard events, callback functions, screen listening, and keeping text predictable.

onkey()listen()strings
Session 1 · Project 13

Keyboard Sketcher

35–45 minutes
1

Map controls

On paper, connect each arrow key to one named function.

2

Build

Bind keys with onkey(), then call listen().

3

Play-test

Ask someone else to draw a letter without touching the mouse.

✓

Done when

All four arrow keys respond, and no movement happens before a key press.

Keyboard controller
from turtle import *

speed(0)

def go_forward():
    forward(20)

def turn_left():
    left(15)

def turn_right():
    right(15)

def clear_page():
    clear()

onkey(go_forward, "Up")
onkey(turn_left, "Left")
onkey(turn_right, "Right")
onkey(clear_page, "space")
listen()
done()
Session 2 · Project 14

Secret Command Console

30–40 minutes
1

Normalize

Predict what " LEFT ".strip().lower() becomes.

2

Build

Accept typed words and turn them into turtle actions with if.

3

Stretch

Use len() to report how many letters were typed.

?

Show & tell

“Why does lowercase make the program more forgiving?”

Command interpreter
from turtle import *

command = input("Type forward, left, or right: ")
command = command.strip().lower()

if command == "forward":
    forward(100)
elif command == "left":
    left(90); forward(100)
elif command == "right":
    right(90); forward(100)
else:
    print("Unknown command:", command)

print("You typed", len(command), "letters.")
done()
Parent cue:If key presses do nothing, click the turtle window once. Then check listen(), key spelling, and whether the callback name has parentheses.
WEEK 08

Build a moving Snake prototype

Core ideas: a game loop, heading, timed updates, screen boundaries, and assembling earlier skills.

whileupdate()game loop
Session 1 · Project 15

One-Segment Snake

40–45 minutes
1

Storyboard a loop

Draw four frames: read direction → move → draw → wait → repeat.

2

Build

Create the screen and snake, bind keys, then move inside a timed loop.

3

Protect direction

Keep the snake from reversing directly into itself.

✓

Done when

The square moves continuously and changes direction from the keyboard.

Playable movement prototype
import turtle
import time

screen = turtle.Screen()
screen.setup(600, 600)
screen.bgcolor("#101820")
screen.title("Snake Prototype")
screen.tracer(0)

snake = turtle.Turtle()
snake.shape("square")
snake.color("#74bd8c")
snake.penup()
snake.direction = "stop"

def go_up():
    if snake.direction != "down":
        snake.direction = "up"

def go_down():
    if snake.direction != "up":
        snake.direction = "down"

def go_left():
    if snake.direction != "right":
        snake.direction = "left"

def go_right():
    if snake.direction != "left":
        snake.direction = "right"

def move():
    x, y = snake.xcor(), snake.ycor()
    if snake.direction == "up": snake.sety(y + 20)
    if snake.direction == "down": snake.sety(y - 20)
    if snake.direction == "left": snake.setx(x - 20)
    if snake.direction == "right": snake.setx(x + 20)

screen.listen()
screen.onkey(go_up, "Up")
screen.onkey(go_down, "Down")
screen.onkey(go_left, "Left")
screen.onkey(go_right, "Right")

while True:
    screen.update()
    move()
    time.sleep(0.12)
Session 2 · Project 16

Boundary Challenge

40–45 minutes
1

Define the rule

Mark the screen edges at ±290. Predict which positions count as “outside.”

2

Build

Add a boundary check inside the loop and reset to the center on collision.

3

Debug by symptom

Too fast? Increase delay. Keys fail? Click the screen and check listen(). Diagonal? Inspect the direction tests.

?

Show & tell

“Which part of the loop reads, changes, and redraws the game state?”

Add this inside the game loop
# Put this after move() inside the while loop:
if (snake.xcor() > 290 or snake.xcor() < -290 or
        snake.ycor() > 290 or snake.ycor() < -290):
    time.sleep(0.5)
    snake.goto(0, 0)
    snake.direction = "stop"
Parent cue:This is a strong prototype, not the full Snake game. Food, growth, score, tail-following, and self-collision belong in the extended Snake completion guide so each idea has room to be learned.

End-of-course demo

Let Alex explain the code he owns.

Choose one mini-project to polish. Alex should make one personal change, show one bug from the notebook, and explain how it was solved. The goal is not perfect code—it is confident cause-and-effect thinking.

Ready for the Snake phase when Alex can…

  • run code and read the final error line;
  • change a variable and predict the result;
  • use a loop for repetition;
  • write and call a small function;
  • explain an if decision;
  • connect a key to a function;
  • describe the game loop in plain English.
